summary: The rule flags else blocks following an if statement whose body contains a breaking statement (return, break, continue, throw), marking them as unnecessary.
firingShapes: for (let i=0; i<n; i++) { if (arr[i]) { continue; } else { sum += arr[i]; } }
try { if (cond) { throw e; } else { log(); } } finally { cleanup(); }
function f() { if (x<0) { return -x; } else { return x; } }
switch(v) { case 1: if (true) { break; } else { doWork(); } default:; }
label: if (flag) { continue label; } else { reset(); }
do { if (stop) { return; } else { process(); } } while (true);
silentShapes: if (a) { return; } else if (b) { c(); } else { d(); }
if (a) { if (b) { return; } else { c(); } } else { d(); }
function f() { if (x) { return; } /* comment */ else { y(); } }
fixDescription: Remove the else block and promote its statements to the same indentation level as the if statement, preserving their original order.
hazards: Moving a var declaration from the else block to the outer scope changes its scoping from block-scoped to function-scoped, potentially causing hoisting issues or name collisions.
If the else block contains a labeled break/continue targeting an outer label, promoting it may alter which loop or switch the label refers to due to changed nesting depth.

Promoting a throw statement from the else block may change exception handling if the if statement was inside a try block whose catch clause no longer captures the thrown value due to altered control flow.
If the else block contains a function declaration, moving it to the outer scope may cause early hoisting and unintended availability before the if statement executes.
When the else block holds a const/let variable that shadows an outer variable, promoting it may cause a syntax error due to duplicate declaration in the same block scope.

Comments attached to the else block (e.g., // comment
else { ... }) may be lost during the rewrite if the tool does not preserve leading or trailing comments on the removed block.
If the if statement is part of a larger conditional chain (e.g., else if), removing the else may incorrectly merge logic or alter the intended branching structure.
Promoting statements from the else block may change evaluation order relative to side effects in the if condition or preceding expressions if those expressions rely on timing.
In strict mode, promoting a with statement from the else block is invalid and will cause a SyntaxError since with is not allowed in strict mode at any scope.
If the else block contains a debugger statement, moving it may alter debugging behavior if tooling associates breakpoints with specific syntactic contexts.
When the else block is empty, the fix removes it entirely, but if it contained only a comment, that comment may be dropped even though it had semantic intent (e.g., TODO or license notice).
If the if condition has a side effect (e.g., function call) and the else block contains a break, promoting the break may cause it to exit a different loop than intended due to altered nesting.
